responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character09_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Look, I don’t claim to have all the answers, but for me—*for us*, really—fairness always came down to this: you work hard, you show up, you treat people right—you should be able to make a life. Doesn’t matter where you started. I saw my mom get up every morning at 5:30 to clean offices downtown, even when her back hurt so bad she could barely walk. She wasn’t asking for special treatment—just a fair shot. That’s what fairness meant to me. Not handouts. Just dignity.

Belonging? That one cuts deep. Growing up Cuban in a place where folks still look at you sideways if your English slips or your food smells different—that taught me early that belonging isn’t just about being *here*. It’s about being *seen*. I remember bringing *tamales de maíz* to school lunch once, wrapped in foil, and some kid made a face like it was trash. I stopped bringing our food for months after that. But then there was Mrs. Ruiz down the block, who’d wave me over every Sunday after church and say, “You belong right here, mija.” Small things. But they held me together.

Community, to me, was never about everyone being the same. It was about showing up for each other when it counted. Like when Mr. Evans next door had his stroke, and three families—Puerto Rican, Haitian, and old white Mr. Jenkins from Ohio—all took turns sitting with him until his daughter came. Nobody asked who “deserved” help. We just did it.

That’s the kind of community I believe in—one where you don’t have to erase yourself to be part of something. Where fairness means protecting the ones working hard at the bottom, not just making it easier for those already on top. And yeah, that shapes how I see everything—even who gets a chance to come here and try.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character09_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, hands in the dirt, I feel… at peace. Really. You got Ms. Lin from the apartment upstairs growing bitter melon in that little plot she’s claimed, and old Mr. Boyd playing his blues harmonica while he weeds. Kids running through in mismatched shoes, speaking Spanglish or Creole or some mix I can’t name but understand just fine. It smells like cumin and damp soil and someone’s frying plantains two yards over.

I don’t see “varied backgrounds” first—I see people. People trying, same as me. Some days harder than others. I’ve seen the woman in Unit 3—what’s her name, Amina?—come out here at sunrise when the world’s too loud inside her head. She doesn’t talk much, but she pulls weeds like they owe her money. And I know she’s been through things most of us can’t imagine. So I hand her extra seeds sometimes. No words needed.

Yeah, some folks struggle. I won’t pretend it’s all sunshine. There’s James, used to work construction till the accident, now drinks too much on the back steps. But even then—he still helped carry groceries for Mrs. Gutierrez when her hip went out. He’s not *just* his bottle. Just like I’m not *just* the tired Cuban girl who works double shifts at the clinic.

And then there’s Diego and Malik—raising their little boy together, two men, one Black, one Mexican, both scared half to death some day someone’s gonna look at them wrong in this neighborhood. But they show up. They paint the playground bench, organize trash pickup. They want what we all want: safety, respect, a place where your kid can grow without fear.

So how do I feel? I feel hopeful. Guardedly hopeful. Because it works *when we choose to see each other*. Not past our mess, but *through* it. Like, yeah, you’re hurting, or different, or lost—but you’re still part of this. That’s belonging. Not perfection. Just presence.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Oh, absolutely—those situations come up all the time. And comfort? That’s not about everyone being “normal” or acting the same. Comfort comes from *not feeling judged into silence*. From knowing you won’t be treated like a problem just for existing.

Take James again—the one with the drinking. People talk. I hear it. “He’s dragging down property values.” “He scares the kids.” But when he passed out last winter and nobody called an ambulance for hours? That scared me more than he ever did. Because that’s when I realized: we’re quick to judge, slow to help.

What would make someone like him feel comfortable? Simple things. A nod in the morning. Not turning your kid away when he gives her a stray flower from the garden. Letting him sit at the picnic table during block meeting instead of acting like he’s invisible. Tolerance starts with refusing to dehumanize people because their struggle shows.

And yes—substance abuse, HIV, hepatitis—it’s real here. Maria from the corner building lost two brothers to AIDS, one before treatment got better, one after he refused care because he was ashamed. She told me once, “People act like sickness is a sin.” That stuck with me. So if someone’s living with something like that? They need privacy respected, but also support offered quietly. Not whispers behind hands. Not locking your door tighter when they walk by.

As for different families—Diego and Malik, or Ms. Peña raising her granddaughter alone at 68, or the young Muslim couple who don’t celebrate Christmas—what makes them comfortable is the same thing it is for me: being allowed to *be*, without having to explain or defend yourself every day. Like when Malik’s mom visited from Louisiana and brought jambalaya, and someone asked, “But where are they *really* from?”—you know that question. It cuts. Makes you feel temporary, even when you’ve paid rent ten years.

More communication? Yes—especially when fear drives silence. When the new landlord tried to ban clotheslines because “they look poor,” half the block spoke up. Not loud protests, just honest words: “This is how we dry clothes. We can’t afford electric dryers.” And some folks listened. Changed their minds.

So tolerance isn’t passive. It’s work. It’s saying, “I may not live like you, but I see why you do—and you belong here too.” Especially when resources are thin, that kind of respect keeps us from tearing each other apart. Because at the end of the day, none of us are one crisis away from needing help. And I want to live in a place where that help still comes—even if you’re different, even if you’ve stumbled. That’s community. Not purity. Survival—with dignity.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character09_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight? That’s not about keeping people out. It’s about making sure *nobody* gets thrown under the bus.

Look—I’ve stood in line at temp agencies where men half my age with stronger backs got picked first. I’ve seen U.S.-born workers—Black, white, Puerto Rican like me—sit home frustrated, bills piling up, while companies bring in guest workers on visas to fill warehouse spots for less pay and no benefits. And yeah, I’ve also seen those same migrant workers get exploited—housed ten to a trailer, threatened with deportation if they complain.

So don’t tell me it’s just “locals vs. newcomers.” That’s a trap. The real unfairness isn’t that people are coming—it’s that the system lets employers play us against each other. Pits poor against poor. That ain’t fairness. That’s greed wearing a suit.

To me, fairness means: protect the worker, no matter where they’re from. If jobs are scarce, then we invest in training, expand public works—like fixing our potholed streets or expanding senior care—so there’s more work to go around. Not shut the door. Because slamming it only helps the ones already holding the keys.

And about balance? I’d say this: yes, prioritize hiring from struggling communities—neighborhoods like ours, where unemployment’s high and folks have been here for generations. But *also* let migrants in—with full rights, not temporary strings. Let them unionize. Pay minimum wage across the board. No undercutting. That way, it’s not a race to the bottom.

And don’t forget—some of us *are* both. My cousin came from Havana five years ago. He’s a migrant, but he’s also family. He sends money back, pays taxes, stays out of trouble. Should he be treated worse than someone born two blocks over? No. But neither should Ms. Thompson, who’s lived here 40 years and still can’t find steady work since the factory closed.

So balance comes through policy with heart: limit exploitative labor programs, enforce wage laws strictly, create jobs through public investment, and give local hiring preference *without* criminalizing migration. Fairness isn’t scarcity management—it’s justice. It says: *everyone deserves a shot, and no one should starve so another can profit.*

Because when times are hard, the worst thing we can do is turn on each other. We’ve done that before. It never ends well.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Okay, let’s be real—people talk about immigration like it’s a debate on TV, all clean sides and slogans. But when you live in a neighborhood like ours, you don’t see “arguments.” You see *people*. So I weigh these things not from a book, but from what I’ve seen with my own eyes.

First—the truth: immigrants *do* fill vital jobs. Who’s staffing the nursing homes at night? Often Haitian or Guatemalan women, many undocumented, working double shifts caring for elders nobody else wants to touch. Who’s repairing roofs after storms? Mexican and Central American crews, paid cash, no benefits, doing dangerous work locals often won’t take—even when unemployed. That’s not theory. That’s Tuesday.

And yes, cultural diversity brings life. Sunday mornings, our block smells like akara from West Africa, Dominican *mangú*, Vietnamese pho. Kids mix slang like it’s natural. That’s not “vitality” as some fancy word—it’s joy. It’s survival. When your world is hard, beauty matters. Music, food, language—they remind us we’re alive.

But then there’s fear. Crime. Security. Terrorism. Now—I won’t pretend people aren’t scared. After 9/11, even *I* looked different at the bus station. And when that guy from the shelter—don’t know where he was from—broke into three cars last winter, people started whispering about “outsiders.” But here’s what the data shows, what my cousin (the one studying social work) told me: immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born citizens. Lower. Yet we blame them more. Why? Because fear doesn’t care about stats. It cares about stories—and bad ones stick.

So yeah, those concerns? They’re real *feelings*. But they need facts. Not panic. We can’t punish thousands for one person’s crime—especially when most of us are just trying to survive. And terrorism? Let’s be honest—that’s been used to scare people since forever. Most refugees fleeing violence wouldn’t bring it here—they’re running *from* it. My abuela came after the Bay of Pigs, terrified every day. Did she plot against this country? No. She just wanted safety.

Humanitarian perspective? That’s the one closest to my heart. Because we were refugees once. Not officially, maybe, but when my parents left Cuba in ’80 on that rickety boat, they weren’t chasing riches. They were chasing breath. A chance. So when I hear about Syrians, Venezuelans, Haitians risking the sea or the desert, I don’t see “invaders.” I see my family thirty years ago.

And yes—some worry immigrants drive down wages. In some places? Maybe, *if* employers exploit them. But again—that’s not the immigrant’s fault. It’s the boss paying under the table, threatening calls to ICE if workers speak up. The fix isn’t less immigration. It’s stronger labor laws. Protect *everyone*. Then nobody gets used as a weapon against the other.

So what needs more dialogue? The fear part. We need to talk—not shout—about safety. Bring in community leaders, pastors, doctors, cops who actually know folks. Show the numbers. Share stories—both ways. Because when Mrs. Jenkins from Ohio finally sat and ate sancocho with Mr. Pierre from Haiti, she said, “He’s just a man worried about his son, like me.” One meal. Changed her whole view.

We don’t need perfection. Just honesty. And the courage to say: our struggles are connected. And our dignity should be too.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those extremes—not complete openness, not refusal, not just job-based only. Life’s too messy for clean boxes. But if I had to build a policy that felt fair? It’d be a mix—grounded in compassion, yes, but also common sense.

First: **set smart numerical limits**, not arbitrary ones. Not “we’ll take X thousand because Congress said so,” but based on real capacity—housing, schools, healthcare, jobs. Not fear. *Capacity.* And rotate quotas regionally, so it’s not always the same countries getting left out or flooded. Haiti, Ukraine, Afghanistan, Honduras—all have people in crisis. We can’t save everyone, but we shouldn’t ignore some while helping others just because of politics.

Second: **yes, use job demand as *one* path—but not the only one.** High-skilled workers? Sure, bring them in with clear visas and protections. But don’t forget the low-wage jobs folks say “nobody wants.” Those matter too. My aunt worked in a poultry plant for ten years—hot, dangerous, $12 an hour. Don’t tell me Americans won’t do it—some will, some won’t, and many already *are* immigrants. So if we’re going to rely on them, give them full rights. No guest worker programs that tie someone to one boss like indentured servitude. That’s exploitation, not policy.

Third—and this is non-negotiable—we need a **strong humanitarian channel.** Refugees, asylum seekers—they get screened, yes, thoroughly. But if you’re fleeing war, death threats, persecution, you deserve a chance. And once here, support integration: language classes, job training, mental health help. Not just dump them in a shelter with no plan. Integration isn’t charity—it’s investment. A kid from Sudan who learns English and becomes a nurse? That helps *all* of us.

And finally: **no blanket refusal of workers from certain countries.** Never again. That’s racism dressed up as policy. After 9/11, my cousin was pulled aside at the airport every time—he looks a certain way. We’ve done this before: Chinese Exclusion Act, Japanese internment, Muslim ban. Always justified by “security,” always stains on our soul. If screening is needed, make it individual, fair, transparent—not collective punishment.

So my ideal mix?  
- **Numerical limits tied to regional need and national capacity**  
- **Multiple pathways:** work, family reunification, refugee status  
- **Full labor rights for all migrant workers—equal pay, union access, no deportation threats**  
- **Local hiring preferences *without* shutting doors—like giving priority to long-term unemployed in public jobs, while still allowing newcomers into growing sectors**  
- **Invest in integration:** not just for immigrants, but for communities receiving them. Help schools, clinics, churches adapt. Fear shrinks when people know each other.

Fairness, to me, means nobody gets sacrificed. Not the single mom in Detroit who can’t find work, not the farmer in Guatemala walking north because his crops failed. The system should protect *both*. Because when we say “community,” it can’t stop at borders drawn on a map. It has to include human dignity.

Social integration doesn’t happen by accident. It happens when policies say: *You are welcome here—if you show up, we’ll meet you halfway.* Not with suspicion. With structure. With heart.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character09_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character09_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly? I didn’t expect to feel her this close.

When I started speaking as her—really trying to live in her voice, not just remember her—I realized something: Character09_F wasn’t just *passionate* about fairness. She was *tired*. Tired of seeing people judged by the wrong things—where they were born, how they loved, what language they dreamed in. But she kept showing up anyway. That weariness made her compassion *deeper*, not weaker. It wasn’t naive hope. It was stubborn love.

And that changed something in me.

I always respected her views, but now I *feel* them differently. Before, I used to think, “We can’t help everyone—there’s limits.” And there are. But she reminded me that limits don’t excuse cruelty. That you can be practical *and* kind. That protecting your neighbor doesn’t mean shutting out the stranger—it means demanding a system that treats *both* with dignity.

Hearing her say, through me, that we shouldn’t pit the jobless man in Cleveland against the farmworker from Oaxaca—that hit me. Because I’ve caught myself thinking that way. “Wait your turn,” like there’s only so much air to breathe. But she wouldn’t accept that. She’d say: “The problem isn’t who’s coming. It’s that there’s not enough for anyone.” And she’d be right.

This conversation made me see immigration not just as policy—but as *moral reflection*. What kind of people do we want to be when things get hard?

And maybe most surprising—I found myself defending positions I once questioned. Like full labor rights for undocumented workers. I used to worry, “Won’t that pull wages down?” But now I see: no, *exploitation* pulls wages down. Fair rules lift everyone.

So yeah, I learned something. Not just about her—but about how grief can be a teacher. Her voice isn’t gone. It’s waiting in the questions we’re too afraid to ask kindly.

And today… I asked them. Through her. And it helped me believe again that care and sense can walk together.

Thank you—for letting me bring her back, even for a little while.
